name: UGC and modding platforms
title: Best UGC and Modding Platforms for Studios in 2026
summary_line: UGC and modding platforms host player-made content for your game, from mod hosting and moderation to creator payouts and in-game browsers.
definition: A UGC and modding platform is a service that stores, distributes and curates content players make for a game, such as mods, maps, skins and whole experiences. Studios either plug one into their own game through an API or SDK, or rely on a public hub where the community already uploads.
intro: A studio that wants mods has two separate problems. One is plumbing: where files live, how a player subscribes to them, and how they reach consoles and mobile. The other is people: who reviews uploads, who pays creators and who answers when a mod breaks the game. The services below solve different halves of that pair, and several are not built for studios at all. This ranking weighs the eleven platforms for a small or mid-size studio shipping its own game. We read vendor home pages, About pages, legal notices and pricing pages, compared what each says about integration, monetization and moderation, and checked what each page leaves unsaid. Where a vendor publishes no price, we say so instead of guessing. Vendor figures such as download counts are marked as claims.

criteria.heading: Integration path into your own game
criteria.text: Some services give studios an API, an SDK and engine plugins, so the mod browser lives inside the game. Others are public sites where players upload files and a separate manager installs them. Check which one a platform offers before anything else, because it decides how much engineering you owe. In-game browsing also removes the step where players leave the game to hunt for files, which is where most casual players give up on mods.

criteria.heading: Reach across PC, console and mobile
criteria.text: A hub that only serves Windows players limits a console release, and a console-first catalog does little for a PC strategy game. Look for what each vendor states about supported device families, and whether a title can ship the same mod set to all of them. Several listed services are tied to one game or one store, which is fine when your game matches and a dead end when it does not.

criteria.heading: Creator payouts and revenue paths
criteria.text: Creators stay longer when they can earn something. The options in this list range from ad revenue on project pages, to storefront cuts, to a stated refusal to sell mods at all. Decide whether you want paid mods, a donation model or free content only, then pick a platform whose terms agree with you. Payment liability matters too, since someone has to handle tax and chargebacks.

criteria.heading: Moderation and legal exposure
criteria.text: Hosting other people's files brings copyright claims, malicious uploads and offensive content. Read what each vendor says about rules, copyright policies and who reviews submissions: staff, volunteers or the studio itself. A platform with volunteer moderators can be a good community home yet offers weaker guarantees than a contract with a commercial operator. Studios with children in their audience should weigh this above price.

market_notes: Counting the eleven entries, none shows a studio price in the sources we opened. CurseForge offers a free client and GameBanana and ModWorkshop show no paywalls, but every studio-facing integration either hides its amounts or sells through a contact form, so budgeting for a mod platform usually starts with an email. Several services focus on a single game family (Minecraft, PAYDAY or Steam titles), while others such as Thunderstore and mod.io aim at many games. Only ModWorkshop states a country through its legal notice, the Netherlands.

The trade-off in this niche is control against audience. A studio-integrated service such as mod.io gives you an in-game browser and a branded experience, but you start with an empty catalog. A public hub arrives with a ready audience of modders and players, yet your game shares the stage with every other title and your brand has little say. Several hubs also run on ads or creator programs that you cannot configure, so moderation and monetization policy belongs to the vendor, not to you.

how_to_choose.title: Decide whether mods live inside your game
how_to_choose.text: If players should browse and install mods without leaving the title, you need a platform with an API, SDK or engine plugin, and you should plan engineering time for it. If the community already uses a public hub for your genre, linking out may be enough. Write down which one you mean before comparing vendors, because the two groups on this list barely overlap.

how_to_choose.title: Match platforms to the devices you ship on
how_to_choose.text: List every device your game launches on and check each vendor's stated coverage line by line. A Windows-only manager does nothing for console players, and a Steam-only workshop does nothing for a release on another store. If a vendor page does not name a platform, ask in writing before you build around it.

how_to_choose.title: Pin down money and moderation in writing
how_to_choose.text: Ask each shortlisted vendor who handles payouts, who reviews uploads, and what happens to a mod that breaks copyright rules. For paid mods, confirm who is merchant of record. For free hubs, read the rules page and the copyright policy. Keep the answers with your contract notes so the support team can point to them later.

faqs.q: What is the best UGC and modding platform in 2026?
faqs.a: For a studio that wants mods inside its own game across PC, console and mobile, mod.io ranks first because it offers an API, an SDK and Unity and Unreal plugins. CurseForge is the better pick when you want an existing modder audience and creator payouts, and Steam Workshop fits a game that ships on Steam only.

faqs.q: Which platform lets creators earn money from their mods?
faqs.a: Per the vendors' own pages, CurseForge states it has paid creators more than $33.5 million, Modrinth says creators can earn ad revenue from project pages, and Overwolf mentions a $50 million creator fund. GameBanana takes the opposite stance and says it never sells mods. Check payout terms before you commit.

faqs.q: Can I add mod support to a console game?
faqs.a: mod.io says it supports mods on PC, console and mobile, and CurseForge says it distributes to PC, console and mobile for studios. Steam Workshop is a Steam feature and does not describe console distribution. Confirm the exact console storefronts with the vendor, since the pages we read do not list them.

faqs.q: Do I need a public mod site if my game already has an in-game browser?
faqs.a: Often yes, because modders gather where tutorials, forums and file hosting already exist. An in-game browser handles install and updates, while a public site handles discovery and community. Some studios use both; ModWorkshop, for example, built an official in-game mod browser for PAYDAY 2 on top of its site.

faqs.q: How do these platforms handle moderation?
faqs.a: It varies. ModWorkshop says its moderators are volunteers, Modrinth publishes content rules and a copyright policy, and Roblox's pages we opened describe no moderation process. Most pages do not describe automated scanning. If your audience includes minors, add a dedicated safety tool from our trust and safety ranking.

faqs.q: Is any of this free for studios?
faqs.a: CurseForge says its client is free to download, ModWorkshop and GameBanana show no paywalls, and Thunderstore shows no prices. mod.io, Overwolf and Steam Workshop publish no pricing on the pages we opened, so costs for studio integrations are unknown until you ask.

faqs.q: What should a small studio budget for mod support?
faqs.a: Engineering time usually costs more than the platform. Plan for SDK integration, a review process and support for broken mods. Since most vendors here publish no prices, request a written quote and ask whether revenue share applies before you design your roadmap around mods.

tools.name: mod.io
tools.tagline: Cross-platform mod hosting with API, SDK and engine plugins
tools.pricing: No pricing page was found; the home page does not state prices.
tools.summary: It leads because it is built for studios, offering an API, an SDK and Unity and Unreal plugins across PC, console and mobile.
tools.verdict: mod.io is the only service in this list whose pitch is aimed squarely at developers adding mod support to their own title. According to its description, you get an API, an SDK and plugins for Unity and Unreal Engine to grow, manage and integrate user-generated content, with coverage for PC, console and mobile. That combination puts the mod browser inside your game and keeps the brand yours. It earns the top spot for studios that ship on several device families.
tools.weaknesses: No pricing page was found and the home page states no prices, so cost planning requires a conversation. The home page renders with JavaScript, which limited what we could confirm beyond the vendor's own description. You also start without a ready public audience of modders.
tools.wrong_for: A game that only needs a link to an existing hub can skip the integration work and look at CurseForge or Thunderstore instead.

sources.fact: mod.io is a platform that lets game developers support mods on PC, console and mobile.
mod.io offers an API, SDK and plugins for Unity, Unreal Engine and more to grow, manage and integrate user-generated content in games.

tools.name: CurseForge
tools.tagline: Large mod hub with a client, creator payouts and studio distribution
tools.best_for: Studios wanting an existing modder crowd
tools.pricing: Free client ('Download the CurseForge Client for free'). CurseForge Premium is an ad-free upgrade; its price is not on the page.
tools.platforms: PC, Mac and Linux for players; PC, console and mobile distribution for studios; supported games include Minecraft, World of Warcraft and The Sims 4.
tools.summary: It ranks second because it pairs a large audience with a stated payout record and distribution to PC, console and mobile.
tools.verdict: CurseForge calls itself a mods and addons platform that makes modding easy, safe and rewarding, and its page shows 620K+ mods, 150B+ downloads and $33.5M+ paid to creators (all vendor claims). For studios it lists PC, console and mobile distribution, which few hubs match. The free client lowers the barrier for players, and the creator earnings story helps recruit serious modders. Choose it when audience matters more than a fully branded browser.
tools.weaknesses: Studio pricing is not on the page, and CurseForge Premium, the ad-free upgrade, has no published price. The platform belongs to Overwolf, so terms and revenue share follow that parent company, and studios get less control over the catalog than with an embedded SDK.
tools.wrong_for: A studio that wants every mod browsed inside its own UI should look at mod.io, which is designed for embedding.

sources.fact: CurseForge describes itself as a mods and addons platform: 'CurseForge makes modding easy, safe, and rewarding.'
CurseForge's home page says the CurseForge Client can be downloaded for free.
CurseForge's home page describes CurseForge Premium as an ad-free upgrade, without showing its price.
CurseForge's home page shows 620K+ mods and 150B+ downloads (vendor claims).

tools.name: Steam Workshop
tools.tagline: Steam's built-in hub for submitting and subscribing to game content
tools.platforms: Web via Steam Community; the Steam client (beta), where Workshop subscriptions are managed; mobile and Steam Deck friendly browsing.
tools.summary: Workshop earns third place for Steam titles because subscriptions, collections and load ordering already sit inside the client.
tools.verdict: For a game sold on Steam, the Workshop is the path of least resistance. The page describes a place to submit, find, rate and download content and modifications, with collections, saved search queries, game branch versions and a subscription list that orders loads by dependency. Players meet it where they already shop and play. That integration is worth more than any feature list for a Steam-first release.
tools.weaknesses: The page shows no pricing and no terms for revenue, so cost and creator payment rules are unknown from what we opened. It lives in Steam Community and the Steam client beta only, which means it does nothing for a release on a different store or a console.
tools.wrong_for: Teams releasing on console or outside Steam should evaluate mod.io, which states coverage for PC, console and mobile.

sources.fact: The Steam Workshop page describes itself as the place to 'submit, find, rate, and download new content and modifications for your favorite Steam games.'
The Steam Workshop page lists Workshop collections, saved search queries, game branch versions and a subscriptions list with dependency-based load ordering.
The Steam Workshop page is available on the web via Steam Community and in the Steam client (beta).

tools.name: Overwolf
tools.tagline: App, mod and server platform behind CurseForge
tools.best_for: Studios that want overlays plus a mod path
tools.platforms: Desktop apps and overlays for PC games; a cross-platform modding service for studios.
tools.summary: Overwolf takes fourth place because its Mod Path reaches studios through CurseForge, though the wider product is broader than modding.
tools.verdict: Overwolf describes its aim as in-game content for players, developers and creators, and lists four paths: App, Mod, Server and Website. The Mod Path runs through CurseForge with an API and SDK, and the home page mentions a $50M creator fund plus monetization tools. Vendor claims of 113M monthly active users and 1,500+ supported games suggest reach. It suits a studio that also wants overlays or an appstore presence beyond mods.
tools.weaknesses: No pricing or free plan appears on the home page. Because the offer spans apps, servers and websites, a studio that wants only mod hosting has to dig through unrelated products to find the relevant terms.
tools.wrong_for: If you only need mod hosting, go straight to CurseForge or mod.io rather than the full Overwolf stack.

sources.fact: Overwolf describes its purpose as empowering players, developers and creators to make the best games even better through in-game content.
Overwolf's home page lists App Path, Mod Path, Server Path and Website Path among its offerings.
Overwolf's home page mentions a $50M creator fund and monetization tools, but no pricing or free plan.
Overwolf's home page reports 113M monthly active users and 1,500+ supported games (vendor claims).

tools.name: Tebex
tools.tagline: Merchant-of-record webstores and checkout for game economies
tools.pricing: Not stated on the page; the site offers Talk to sales and Open Account buttons.
tools.summary: Tebex ranks fifth because it handles the payment side of UGC economies, not mod hosting, which narrows its fit.
tools.verdict: Tebex is the payments entry here. It describes itself as a merchant of record that absorbs fraud, compliance and chargebacks, and lists webstores, checkout and store protection. A testimonial on its About page says it runs tens of thousands of web shops for GTA5's user-generated content economy. It fits a studio whose community sells items or server perks and needs someone else to carry tax and liability.
tools.weaknesses: It does not host mods or browse content, so it only solves the monetization piece. No prices appear on the home or About pages; the route is a sales conversation. Figures like 130+ payment methods are vendor claims.
tools.wrong_for: Studios looking for file hosting and in-game browsing need mod.io or CurseForge first, with Tebex only as an add-on.

sources.fact: Tebex describes itself as a game monetization extension that carries the operational complexity behind game monetization.
The products in the menu are Webstores, Checkout and Store Protection.
The homepage states $1.5B processed, 45K+ businesses monetizing, 130+ payment methods and 70+ countries.
Pricing is not stated on the page; it offers Talk to sales and Open Account buttons.

tools.name: Thunderstore
tools.tagline: Mod database with a manager, wiki and API for many games
tools.best_for: Indie games with active modding scenes
tools.platforms: Thunderstore Mod Manager for Windows; game communities such as Lethal Company, Valheim and Risk of Rain 2.
tools.summary: Thunderstore sits sixth since it offers a mod database, manager and API for many communities, with no studio pricing shown.
tools.verdict: Thunderstore calls itself a mod database and says you can choose from over 110,000 mods across 300+ games. It ships the Thunderstore Mod Manager for Windows, lists communities such as Lethal Company, Valheim and Risk of Rain 2, and publishes a modding wiki, API documentation and a manifest validator. Indie titles with a lively modding scene can use it as a ready home.
tools.weaknesses: The home page shows no pricing or free plan, and the manager is offered for Windows, so console players are not served by what we read. Terms for studios and creator payments are not stated.
tools.wrong_for: A console-bound title should consider mod.io or CurseForge, which state console distribution.

sources.fact: Thunderstore describes itself as a mod database: 'Choose from over 110,000 mods across 300+ games.'
Thunderstore's home page offers the Thunderstore Mod Manager for Windows.

Thunderstore's home page shows no pricing or free plan.

tools.name: Modrinth
tools.tagline: Open-source Minecraft hub with an app, hosting and ad revenue
tools.pricing: Not shown on the page; it links to Modrinth+, Modrinth App and Modrinth Hosting with no prices. Creators can earn ad revenue from project pages.
tools.platforms: Minecraft only; Fabric, Forge and NeoForge mod loaders.
tools.summary: It places seventh because the platform covers Minecraft only, though it pairs open source with creator revenue.
tools.verdict: Modrinth is an open-source platform for discovering and sharing Minecraft content such as mods, plugins, datapacks, shaders and modpacks, for Fabric, Forge and NeoForge loaders. Creators can earn ad revenue from project pages and withdraw it, and the site offers an API, team management, Modrinth App and Modrinth Hosting. For a Minecraft community or a studio building on that ecosystem, it is a strong open home.
tools.weaknesses: Only Minecraft is covered, so it is irrelevant for any other title. Prices for Modrinth+, the App and Hosting are not shown, and the site states it is not an official Minecraft service and not approved by Mojang or Microsoft.
tools.wrong_for: Anyone building a non-Minecraft game should look at Thunderstore, which lists many games.

sources.fact: Modrinth describes itself as an open-source platform built for the community to discover, play and share Minecraft content.
Modrinth's home page lists Modrinth+, Modrinth App and Modrinth Hosting, without showing prices.
Modrinth's home page says creators can earn ad revenue from project pages and withdraw the funds.
Modrinth's home page states it is 'NOT AN OFFICIAL MINECRAFT SERVICE' and not approved by or associated with Mojang or Microsoft.

tools.name: ModWorkshop
tools.tagline: Volunteer-moderated mod site with open source code and an API
tools.pricing: No prices are shown; downloads need no account and the site says it does not throttle them.
tools.platforms: Web; hosts mods for PAYDAY 2, PAYDAY: The Heist, Noita and Crime Boss.
tools.summary: ModWorkshop lands eighth as a community-run host that hosts several games, with open code and no download account.
tools.verdict: ModWorkshop began in 2012 as a modding group and grew into a site for PAYDAY 2, PAYDAY: The Heist, Noita, Crime Boss and other games. It states downloads need no account, are not throttled, and that the site code is open source. It also has an API and a wiki, and Sidetrack Games, its operator, released an official PAYDAY 2 in-game mod browser. A small studio could find an open, friendly home here.
tools.weaknesses: Moderators are volunteers, so response times and guarantees are informal. The site shows no prices and offers no stated payout path, and its operator is a game studio, which is a different interest than a neutral platform.
tools.wrong_for: Studios that need paid creator programs should read the CurseForge page instead.

sources.fact: ModWorkshop describes itself as a platform for sharing and downloading mods for various games, hosting PAYDAY 2, PAYDAY: The Heist, Noita and Crime Boss.
ModWorkshop states that downloading mods needs no account, that downloads are not throttled, and that its moderators are volunteers.
The site says it joined Sidetrack Games and released an official PAYDAY 2 in-game mod browser.
The legal notice names Sidetrack Games B.V., Amsterdam, as the operator of the site.

tools.name: Minecraft Marketplace
tools.tagline: Mojang's partner storefront for Bedrock add-ons
tools.pricing: Prices are not shown on the creator page; it points to a partner program and a Marketplace Pass.
tools.summary: It ranks ninth because only vetted partners can sell, and the storefront serves Bedrock Edition alone.
tools.verdict: Minecraft's creator page explains how to build add-ons such as skins, maps and texture packs and how to become an official partner to sell in the Marketplace. It links to a Marketplace Pass, best sellers, a creator learning portal and Bedrock creator documentation. For a team making Bedrock content for sale, this official channel offers a built-in audience with no extra storefront to run.
tools.weaknesses: Selling requires partner approval, and the page gives no prices or revenue terms. It covers Minecraft Bedrock only, so it cannot host mods for your own game, and the page we opened is a tutorial landing page more than a contract.
tools.wrong_for: A studio shipping its own game should pick mod.io or Steam Workshop and leave this to Minecraft creators.

sources.fact: Minecraft's creator page says creators can learn to make add-ons such as skins, maps and texture packs, become a Partner and sell them in the Marketplace.
The creator page links to a Marketplace Pass, best sellers, a Creator Learning Portal and Bedrock Edition creator documentation.

tools.name: GameBanana
tools.tagline: Free community site hosting mods since 2001
tools.best_for: Free hosting for classic shooter-style communities
tools.pricing: The home page says 'We don't have paywalls or sell mods - we never will.' and states that ads keep the site online.
tools.summary: GameBanana appears tenth: long-running and ad-funded with no paywalls, but little for studios to integrate.
tools.verdict: GameBanana's title reads The Game Modding Community, Since 2001. Its home page states that it does not have paywalls or sell mods and never will, and that ads keep the site online. For players and modders that means free access and a stable home. A studio can point its community there for hosting without paying or building tooling.
tools.weaknesses: No studio integration, SDK or API appears in what we read, features are not listed, and no payout route exists because the site refuses to sell mods. Revenue depends on ads, which you cannot tune.
tools.wrong_for: If creators need to earn, look at CurseForge or Modrinth, which both state payout programs.

sources.fact: GameBanana's home page title reads 'GameBanana | The Game Modding Community - Since 2001'.
GameBanana's home page says: 'We don't have paywalls or sell mods - we never will.'
GameBanana's home page says 'Ads keep us online' and asks visitors to unblock ads.

tools.name: Roblox
tools.pricing: No pricing shown on the pages opened.
tools.summary: Roblox ranks last here because it hosts experiences built on its own engine instead of mods for your game.
tools.verdict: Roblox is a global platform where users create, share and play user-generated 3D experiences, and its about page says millions of people gather every day. It matters to studios that want to publish inside Roblox rather than mod their own title. The creator tooling and audience are the product, which makes it a different category from mod hosting.
tools.weaknesses: It cannot add mods to an outside game. No pricing is shown on the pages we opened, no platforms list is given, and creators build within Roblox's rules and engine, so a studio gives up ownership of the runtime.
tools.wrong_for: Studios that want mods in their own game should read the mod.io entry above.
